newsitem.title: UK: Economists voice doubts over EMU timetable.
newsitem.headline: Economists voice doubts over EMU timetable.

text.p: Leading commercial bank economists on Tuesday expressed nagging doubts over whether European economic and monetary union (EMU) would make its planned January 1, 1999 launch date.
Speaking in a panel discussion at a bond conference in London, four of five economists at major banks said the chance of it happening on time was near 50-50.
"The odds are against it happening on time," HSBC Group chief economist Roger Bootle told the conference of some 1,500 delegates from approximately 50 countries.
"Monetary union is an economic gamble," he said, although when asked to give a figure during a panel discussion he rated the chance at 50-50.

Bootle said the Italian economy had performed well in its efforts to meet criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty, but there were risks to the EMU process if Germany decided to oppose Italy's participation in the first wave of EMU.
The Italian government has been steadfast in its ambition to be among the first participants of a single euro currency, but there have been doubts in financial markets that it will make the grade.
Nikko Europe chief UK economist Simon Briscoe agreed, giving the probability of EMU happening on time a 50-50 chance.
"There are still hurdles to overcome," he said, adding it was possibly more important to focus on 2002, when national notes and coins for member countries are due to be withdrawn.
Under EMU, member currencies are to be fixed at irrevocable rates on January 1, 1999 but they will still run side-by-side with the euro until 2002.
"1999 is yet another version of fixed exchange rates," Briscoe said.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell chief economist Steven Bell said the probability of EMU happening on time was 55 percent. He referred to the inclusion of southern European countries as a "dilemma".
UBS Ltd chief international economist George Magnus was marginally more optimistic and gave the likelihood of EMU happening on time a 60 percent chance. "But the percentage is falling," he said.
"The waxing and waning (of whether EMU will happen on time or not) will continue," Magnus said, adding: "Germany is both the strongest and weakest link in the chain."
The most bullish was CSFB chief economist Giles Keating.
With tongue-in-cheek he told the conference the chance of EMU going ahead on time was precisely "91.783 percent". But he said there would still be waves of uncertainty in the market.

Bank of England executive director Ian Plenderleith was included in the panel discussion. He declined to give a figure as to the probability of EMU happening on time, but advised delegates to plan their business with EMU in mind.
"It's on the cards and won't go off the agenda," he said.
"Plan on the euro coming into being, even if there is an adjustment in timing, it will come along sooner of later."
Britain, which has an "opt-out" clause on EMU, remains officially undecided about whether to participate in a single currency.
